en: The *Vīraśaiva-siddhāntottara-kaumudī* (The Moonlight of the Ultimate Tenets of Vīraśaivism).
[The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Śiva]

O bestower of the knowledge of Śiva, you who are the form of a raft for crossing the terrible ocean of saṃsāra— difficult to traverse due to its vast waves of attachment to sense objects, its whirlpools of delusion, and its heat from the submarine fire ignited by Madana, who was revived after being consumed by the blazing flames of the eye on the forehead of the glorious Rudra; O enemy of the senses, who are like a row of lotuses to greed!

O Guru of initiation, who bestows the knowledge of Śiva— the axe that cuts through the dense forest of saṃsāra, which is characterized by great calamities such as the demon of delusion, the tiger of anger, the serpent of pride, the thief of passion, the darkness of intoxication, the three-fold heat of suffering, the thorns of sense-objects, the poisonous creeper of envy, and the venomous pit of egoism.

Having requested, "Please grant me the instruction for the purpose of worshipping you," and having performed prostrations with long staffs (dīrghadaṇḍa-namaskāra), he placed the articles of worship there and grasped the big toes of the Guru's feet.
The Guru’s form is Śiva manifest, the supreme Śiva liberated from bonds;
within his pair of feet abide the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Indeed, sixty-eight sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell upon the tip of the big toe,
and the hosts of lunar mansions and planets truly reside in his ankle.
The seven oceans reside in the half-foot, and the principal mountain ranges in its half;
in the two shanks, the multitude of thirty-six principles dwells eternally. Thus [it is said].
Having prostrated and applied the sacred ash (bhasma), and having performed the rites of bathing and other services right there with various kinds of flowers and fragrant, variegated garlands,
one should establish the form of the venerable Guru and worship it at every joint.

Having worshipped all the joints with these words, having performed all the ritual services (*upacāra*), and having set aside the flowers and so forth; having washed the entire foot—starting from the ankle downwards and including the big toe—as indicated by the word "foot" (*pāda*); having placed it in a vessel such as a conch shell; and having fully worshipped it.

One might ask: what is meant by "water from the feet" (*pādodaka*)? Even in the *Śaivasiddhāntaśikhā*, it is stated that for one who has taken refuge in the station of the devotee (*bhaktasthala*), the acceptance of grace (*prasāda*) is prescribed among the fifteen stations; however, the drinking of water from the feet is not mentioned there.
Anticipating this doubt, it is stated in that very same work that the acceptance of the water from the feet occurs precisely prior to the reception of grace.
Regarding the greatness of the water for washing the feet (*pādodaka*) and the fruits of its consumption, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"The non-dual knowledge that arises during initiation between the teacher and the disciple—
the bliss that flows forth from that is known as the *pādodaka* of initiation."
Supreme bliss alone, being stainless, is expressed by the word "foot" (pāda);
knowledge is expressed by the word "water" (udaka); thus it is remembered as "pādodaka" (the water of the feet).
Alternatively, the word *pāda* refers to the Guru, and the word *udaka* refers to the disciple; their unity, however, is achieved through initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Having attained the contemplation of supreme bliss, whose nature is the light of the consciousness of the Other,
the great yogi perceives no duality anywhere.
"Having tasted the nectar of knowledge—pure and born of the Guru's compassion—the yogi rejoices, freed from the maladies of saṃsāra. Thus it is said.

Then: Salutations to the one whose essence is Śiva, who has arisen from the lotus-feet of both the Linga and the mobile [form], who is the nature of supreme bliss, and who is like the sacred water at the feet.

Thus, having prostrated before the water for the feet (*pādodaka*), and having correctly understood the ritual forms such as the offering of the bath-water (*majjana-arpaṇa*) and so forth, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the water from the Guru’s feet, just like the acceptance of the water from the lotus-feet of Śiva. Just as one accepts the water from the feet of Maheśvara with devotion...
Likewise, [there is] the eternal [identity] of Śiva and the Self, and also of the Guru and the Jaṅgama.

And in the *Śikṣāpādodaka*, it is said: "From the ocean of the Teacher’s scriptures, through the power of the churning-staff of reasoning, the nectar of awakening is obtained by the hosts of wise ones under the guidance of the Guru."

Thus, by the statement "for those who follow the devotees," it is understood that when there is a large multitude, the sacred water (*tīrtha*) is small; if it is mixed with [ordinary] water, a great fault arises. As it is said: "The water from the feet of the Supreme Brahman is stainless and destroys poverty; yet if that which is non-inert is mixed with the inert, one becomes a sinner."

"Belonging to the realm of Brahman. Thus, when there are many groups [of initiates], the distinction is that for both [the stationary and mobile forms] there is indeed only one [portion] from other vessels.

Following that is the acceptance of the *prasāda*. From the acceptance of the *prasāda* of the Śiva-liṅga, what fruit may arise? Likewise, the acceptance of the *prasāda* applies to the Guru and the *jaṅgama* as well.

One should cause [the disciple] to consume the *prasāda* that has been purified by speech or has fallen there. Salutations again and again to the *prasāda* arisen in its threefold form: as the Great Linga, as the Great Mobile [form], and as the third.
"As pure *liṅga* (the phallus), the face is abandoned; as *siddha*, it is devoid of movement;
as *prasiddha*, it is that which has been consumed by the Guru—thus there are three kinds of *prasāda*," so it is said in the *Vīrāgama*.
Furthermore, Āpastamba states: "That which he eats as leavings is indeed the leavings of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Therefore...

One should perform the worship of the *liṅga*. Then, having recited the hymn to the Guru and performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should recite the six-syllabled mantra preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). It is as follows:
[the great six-syllabled mantra] of this venerable Six-Station Brahman (*ṣaṭsthalabrahma*).

The seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra is the Supreme Brahman; the meter (chandas) is the divine Gāyatrī; the deity (devatā) is Śiva; the power (śakti) is Maheśvarī; the seed-syllable (bīja) is Hrīṃ; the pin (kīlaka) is Hrauṃ. [This six-syllabled mantra is for] the cessation of the six waves (ṣaḍūrmi) and other afflictions within my body, and for the attainment of the blissful wealth of the Nirvāṇa-Brahman in the six locations (ṣaṭsthala). The six-syllabled [mantra].

I shall perform the recitation of the great mantra (*mahāmantra*). *Yaṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Vāṃ* to the two index fingers, *namaḥ*. *Śiṃ* to the two middle fingers, *namaḥ*. *Maṃ* to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*.
*Naṃ* to the two little fingers, *namaḥ*. *Ūṃ* between the hands. *Ūṃ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Yaṃ on the head; vāṃ on the face; śiṃ on the heart; maṃ on the navel; naṃ on the two feet.

Ūṃ, obeisance to the syllable Ūṃ, the heart; svāhā to the syllable Na, the head; vaṣaṭ to the syllable Ma, the crest-lock; huṃ to the syllable Śi, the armor; vauṣaṭ to the syllable Va, the three eyes.

*Yakārāyāstrāya phaṭ*. With *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaroṃ*, there is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). The meditation (*dhyāna*): *Oṃ namaḥ śivāgnibījāya harāya paramātmane |* *Ūṃ-antamantrarūpāya mūlapañcākṣarātmane ||* *Ūṃ-kāra-vadanā devi vakāra-bhujadvayā |* *Śikāra...* [Salutation] to the seed-syllable of Śiva-fire, to Hara, the Supreme Self; to the one whose form is the mantra ending in *oṃ*, whose essence is the five-syllabled root-mantra. O Goddess, you have the syllable *ūṃ* as your face and the syllable *va* as your two arms. [The syllable] *śi*...

The supreme five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*), consisting of the two words "Namaḥ" and "Kāra" situated in the center of the body, together with the Star (Tārā), is the form of the Liṅga. This Śaiva mantra, known as the mantra of Śiva, is firmly established within my limbs.
It is the six-sthalas Brahman, the deity of the six-syllabled mantra, the Mother, and the devotion to the six sthalas.
Salutations to you, the sole bestower of the supreme bliss of serene faith.
Having meditated thus, having applied ashes to the palms of the hands, having prepared the seat of the Praṇava (Oṃ), and having installed the Liṅga,
one should become engaged in the recitation of the six-fold Śrī-Ṣaḍakṣarī Vidyā— which embodies the six locations— and which consists of the fourfold modes of conduct beginning with Parā,
as well as the six locations beginning with devotion.
Having thus made this request for the purpose of illuminating the specific meaning,
and having bowed to the lineage of gurus who have reached the further shore of the goal of Śiva-vidyā and are fully perfected within the inner self of Śiva;
The Guru, who is the embodiment of the six-syllabled Vidyā and consists of the six sacred sites (ṣaṭsthala).
Having bowed to the perfected state of the Guru’s feet, which is the highest good, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Of this six-syllabled mantra of the Śrī-Ṣaṭsthalabrahman, the Seer (Ṛṣi) is Parabrahman;
the metre (Chandas) is said to be the Śaiva Gāyatrī; and its Deity is Śiva himself, while his Power (Śakti) is considered to be Māheśvarī.
The seed-syllable is joined with Māyā and the Bindu, conjoined with the two [Śiva and Agni];
Kīlala is endowed with Śiva and Vahni and possesses fourteen Kalās.
Combined with the bindu, its application is now described.
While I am still embodied here, for the cessation of the six waves and other afflictions,
and for the attainment of the wealth of bliss in the Nirvāṇa of Brahman through the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), [I seek refuge].
O Śiva, I shall perform the recitation of the six-syllable mantra for the sake of the sacrifice.
One should place the syllable *praṇava* in the center of the two five-fingered hands, from the thumb to the little finger, and then assign the letters in their proper sequence.
One should assign the mantras *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* to the heart and other limbs;
these, joined with the dative case, are preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the offering of oneself (*ātmarpaṇa*), and having further applied the ritual application (*viniyoga*), [one should recite]:
"Obeisance to Śiva, the seed-syllable of fire, to Hara, the Supreme Self."
To her whose form is the mantra *Ūṃ*, whose essence is the five-syllable root mantra;
the Goddess whose face is the syllable *Ūṃ*, whose two arms are the syllable *Vā*,
whose middle body is the syllable *Śi*, and whose two feet are the syllable *Namaḥ*.
The five-syllabled supreme knowledge, together with the Tārā, embodied as the Liṅga,
the Śaiva mantra named after Śiva, is established within my limbs.

"O you who are the embodiment of Brahman in the six locations, the deity of the six-syllabled mantra, the Mother, the bestower of the singular supreme bliss through the grace of devotion to the six locations— salutations to you! Having thus obtained permission from her, one should mutter the auspicious five-syllabled mantra.
The venerable six-syllabled mantra, which possesses seven stars and consists of six locations, is the embodiment of Brahman.
This Śaiva knowledge is fourfold: Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī;
it is further divided according to meaning, phonemes, words, and sentences.
Omartha is not Ādiyā; its color there is two-fold and threefold.
That which is the aggregate of those [words] becomes a *pada*; it is designated as a *vākya* (sentence).
The supreme knowledge (parā vidyā) has the form of meaning; Paśyantī has the form of phonemes (varṇa); Madhyamā would have the form of words (pada); and Vaikharī has the form of sentences (vākya).

Meaning arises from the mind, color from the eye, and the word from speech; the sentence arises from the body. Among these—mind, eye, speech, and body—their characteristics should be known in sequence: the characteristic of the mind is the act of thinking.
Her face is marked by the glances of her eyes, and her speech is characterized as being like the mere ether.
The characteristic of the union of the palate, lips, and tongue is called the body (vapuḥ). It is fivefold:
mental, visual, external, vocal, and corporeal.
These are called, in sequence, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.

This bearer of fragrance, perfumed by *prāṇāyāma*, abides in internal *samādhi*. The vital breath (*prāṇa*), from the sense-organ of smell, moves outward as the non-self; its movement is thus described.

In the ritual of recitation pertaining to Śambhu, you, who act according to your own conduct, should always abide with supreme devotion in the place of your devotees and worship the Liṅga known as Cārākhya.

Devoted to the worship of the Guru-liṅga, which is the very essence of the six-syllabled mantra, he remains steadfast in his own tongue; or else, in the sacred precincts of Maheśvara, he performs the recitation. With unblinking eyes, gazing with focused attention upon the Śiva-liṅga as his own cherished form, he himself always chants.
Devoted to worship at the site of grace,

he constantly worships the mobile *liṅga* shining through the gateway of the sense of touch by means of tactile recitation (*sparśana-jāpya*). Thus, he remains in this state of one who possesses the vital-force *liṅga*, which is knowable solely through his own direct experience.

The ear-organ, situated in the mouth—the abode of the arrow—worships the dense *liṅga* of grace, which consists of the nectar of the sound of mantra-recitation from the chanting; it does so as it becomes filled with mature bliss.
Performing service to the great Liṅga, whose form is the meaning of the mantra, by means of constant mental reflection day after day through awakening,
one indeed knows nothing else at all due to that state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).
In the state of supreme excellence, this is established as the absorption of recitation (japa-samādhi).
Where there is the movement of the vital breath (*marut*), there is the mind (*manas*); where there is the mind, there is the application of the vital breath.
Here, however, it is the six-syllabled mantra alone, and not anywhere else—thus does one recite the *Ṣaṭsthalī*.

The sound "sīt" is the worship of the Support; the ritual of recitation is the firm embrace with arms entwined; the counting of beads on the hand is the casting of the Śiva-beads (rudrākṣas) upon the great courtyard; the agitation is the activity appropriate for sexual union;
the bed is indeed the lotus posture (padmāsana); and the conversation is the five-syllabled mantra uttered softly.
O you who are well-integrated!
O Māyā, O lady of excellent limbs, the supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā) has reached its highest state and delights me day and night; there is no room for you to sport with me.
Having thus prescribed the practice of lower knowledge (aparavidyā),

one should then [worship] the liṅga of vital breath (prāṇaliṅga), which consists of higher knowledge (parāvidyā), within the lotus of the heart— adorned with three circles— among the locations of the mūlādhāra, the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), because the heart is the most excellent.

Having correctly contemplated the state (*bhāva*), one should worship with the flowers of that state. As it is said: "The supreme *liṅga* consisting of Śiva, which is the internal form of consciousness, is worshipped by the flowers of the state; for that indeed is the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*."

The characteristics of the *tallakṣaṇa* are described in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*: bathing is equanimity; clothing is the state of fullness with water; the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) is endowed with the three powers and qualities;
fragrance is spiritual knowledge; unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) are compassion for all beings; and flowers are sound and the other objects of the senses.
O Goddess, always bestow this upon my limbs.

The embodied being offers as an oblation the intellect, mind, ego, and consciousness as incense; the five sense organs, such as hearing, as the lamp; the body, joined with the oil of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as the wick; and external pleasure and pain as the sacrificial offering.
The betel-roll called the three qualities, the offering of life, prostration,
the handful of flowers for peace, and the dismissal with single-minded devotion.
Having thus performed the inner worship, known as the internal sacrifice consisting of the enumeration of internal substances for the adoration of Śiva,
one should sprinkle one’s own *iṣṭaliṅga* with sacred ash using the root mantra and gaze upon that *liṅga* with the ten attentions (*daśāvadhāna*).
At the outset, ten attentions (avadhānas) were taught for the worship of Śiva;
first among them is the fourfold gaze, wherein the clarity of that gaze is essential.
The light of consciousness situated at the tip of the hand, sustained by the sight, mind, and vital breath, is the Linga depicted in the sacrificial pit of vision;
it is called the Linga whose form is vision itself.
Just as a statue made of iron acquires its form through association with a goldsmith,
so too is this clarity of vision and the arrangement of the gaze described.
One should behold that moment of Śiva in his triple form, just like Guheśa.
Free from blinking, one should gaze upon the Lord as if without blinking;
with the multitude of qualities transcended, one should see as Bhṛṅgīśvara does.
One should perceive Śiva through the principle of inseparable connection, just as Nandīśvara did.

The placement of the gaze has been described right here; likewise, the dissolution of the gaze is now explained. Just as the series of mantras spoken by the Guru dissolve into the two ears of the disciple, so too the gaze fixed on the tips of the fingers shall go to dissolution within the *cilliṅga*.
The meaning of Vedānta bestows auspiciousness, and likewise, the eye bestows the Lord;
as the wish-fulfilling tree is enveloped by creepers, so too is Śiva bound by the gaze.
Just as [the thread] was sewn upon the forehead, so was it sewn upon the lord of the eyes;
and having seen this, Śiva was embraced by his sons and father.
Just as hunters bind a scent-elephant with a snare, so is Śiva bound by his own glances;
just as a net set by a hunter binds a deer, so does the glance bind him.

The husband was embraced by his wife, and likewise Śiva was embraced by her gaze; just as a cloth is fashioned from threads according to the pattern by a craftsman, or as a painting is formed with fragrant substances;
just as rivers merge into the ocean, or as water is absorbed into milk.
Just as water on heated iron, or as [an object] dissolved in the vision of Śiva;
the stability of vision, however, will be described as the fourth, though it is situated in the first.
The primordial wisdom, which does not turn back and which bears the waters of the limbs of mental application,
shall today be free from flickering for me, and thereafter there shall be no further movement.
This steadiness of the gaze, which possesses the quality of being bodiless and is not cruel,
is thus called the first of the fourfold types of vision regarding the *liṅga*.
Beholding Śiva, they attain happiness by beholding him in manifold ways;
this second stage of focused attention consists of the eightfold perfect worship of his vision.
The vision [of the deity] takes the form of immersion in water; the vision consists of incense, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
the vision is the offering of flowers; the vision is that which has the form of incense smoke;
the vision is known as the waving of lights (nīrājana); and the vision is the very nature of the food offering (naivedya).
The gaze shall take the form of betel-leaf, and the gaze shall become an offering of flowers;
thus, through the focused application of the gaze, the worship of the Lord is indeed accomplished.
By the mere sight of the Liṅga, one should drink the nectar of the eightfold gaze.
But when it is pervaded by vision, it becomes the third; thus is its focused attention described:
just as a poor man [conceals] a deposit, or as one who possesses an elephant [guards] a female elephant.
Just as Śiva touches his play-lotus and Gaurī’s husband touches his wife’s breast, so too did the image repeatedly touch Śambhu, while Cūti herself [touched it].
One experiences auspicious and pleasant touch through the very act of touching Śiva; one experiences auspiciousness through various kinds of hymns, whether born of the Vedas or the Purāṇas.
Having praised [Śiva] with the hymns declared in the *Raudropaniṣad*, one shall attain the bliss of praise;
indeed, this fourth stage of meditative absorption consists of the form of Śiva’s praise.
The body, along with the sense objects and the senses, completely dissolves into the *liṅga*,
just as butter [dissolves] in fire or camphor in a lamp.
Like salt in water, and likewise like a stone in the ocean, it remains for a year.
Thus, worship is always performed by those who have transformed their limbs;
this is indeed the fifth form of worship, and now the pervasion of the mind is described.
The tears of joy shall be the bath, and the drops [of sweat] shall be the unguent for rubbing the body.
Scent is her delight, respectful service is her flower garland, horripilation is her manifestation of reality, and sacred ash is her divine fragrance; incense is her own exquisite perfume.
A portion of knowledge is the array of lamps, the vital breath is the food offering,
transcendence of the senses is the betel leaf, and the hymn of praise shall be the handful of flowers.

One should perform the acts beginning with bathing and culminating in the offering of handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), preceded by meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), while maintaining focused attention on the distinctions of the visualized forms.
During the ritual services such as bathing, the mind should attain identity with that [divine] form;
during the immersion, however, the mind experiences itself as a stream of water.
In worship, the fragrance is the mind, the application of scent is the mental faculty; in incense, it is the nature of mental impressions, while the lamp is auspiciousness and its light is delight.
But when offering pleasing food oblations, the mind experiences six kinds of flavors.
At the time of bathing the mind, it takes the form of the water used for immersion.

At the time of worship, he takes the form of an offering of flowers; at the time of offering incense, he takes the form of fragrance; at the time of offering incense-sticks, he takes the form of smoke; at the time of offering a lamp, he takes the form of light; and at the time of offering food, he takes the form of whatever is pleasing to [the deity]. This too is born of the mind.
Thus the sixth worship has been described; the mind is the worship characterized by passion.
Having seen the Gaṇas born of devotion to Śiva in the midst of Śiva,
one should personally bow down to those innumerable ones with the *Gaṇarudrānuvākas*.
One should perform a hymn of praise after meditating upon the Gaṇas situated with Śiva through the Rudra-sūktas:
"He who is called the one Rudra—countless thousands are remembered, but he is not seen."

Thus, O celestial hosts of many forms and ancient ones, understand this: "Homage be to the blue-necked one, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful; and also to those who are his attendants—to them I offer homage. Homage to the piercing ones," and he should utter the end [of the formula]: "and to the dog-leaders. Homage to you!

Homage to the piercing hearts of the gods! Homage to the searching hearts of the gods! Homage to the unassailable hearts of the gods! Homage to the consuming hearts of the gods! In the full ocean of the play of the Gaṇas, overflowing with bliss...

The sun, moon, planets, stars, and so forth do not sink into this great ocean of the atmosphere; rather, having attained eightfold sovereignty upon the surface of the earth, they cause wonder, for even the Blessed Lord Śiva is constantly amazed by their deeds. Into this vast ocean of the intermediate space, I cast that seed for you, which is the source of differentiation.
Thus, the ninth [chapter], "Immersion in the Ocean of the Play of the Gaṇas," comes to an end.
With the mind dissolved in Śiva, one sees nothing other than Śiva;
"I am subtler than the subtle, and likewise I am the Great One—this entire universe in its manifold variety."

"I am of the nature of Śiva. Reciting such non-dualistic scriptures as "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one thereafter attains immortality," he ascends to the station of the hundred-fold heights.
The Liṅga is mounted by both vision and the mind, both externally and internally.
The entire universe, whether seen by the eye or remembered by the mind, consists of the *liṅga*;
therefore, the whole world is itself the *liṅga*, for there is not even an atom that is not so.
Having thus performed the ten attentions (*avadhāna*), one should perform the worship (*pūjā*).
All of this has been correctly described by Cāritrapaṇḍita, who was propitiated by Somārādhya, in the *Śivārcanasamyajña*. Following these ten attentions, there is the *darśana* and the *nīrājana*.
O Sadāśiva, O Lord, you who abide within and pervade without in the form of the Jyotirliṅga,
accept this waving of lights known as the vision [of the deity].

Having offered the *nīrājana* of vision with this mantra, having applied sacred ash (*bhasma*) to the *liṅga*, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) from the *pādya* vessel to the feet, having offered water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) from the *arghya* vessel to the hands, and having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) from the *ācamana* vessel to [the mouth].
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the water from the vessel for relinquishment (*tyāga-pātra*), and having filled and offered that vessel of flowing water; then,
having sprinkled the water from the *liṅga* onto one's head with the mantra "Obeisance to Śambhu" (*namaḥ śambhave ca*),
[one performs] the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self, with water such as hot water and so forth.

"One performs this [rite] called *liṅgodaka*," so it is remembered in the Smṛti. Immediately after that, having wiped [the feet] with a cloth and performed the application of ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*), one should visualize the two feet upon the pedestal beneath the Liṅga. Having paid obeisance and worshipped thoroughly, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) using the water from the vessel of knowledge (*jñānapātra*), and [collect] the water from the feet into the *pādya* vessel.

Having taken that vessel and worshipped it, one should consecrate it with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge" and perform the sprinkling over the head with the two mantras "kadrudrāya" and "mā tvā rudra". Then, one should offer obeisance: "Obeisance to the Self of Śiva, who has arisen from the lotus feet of the Liṅga and the Jaṅgama, and whose form is supreme bliss; obeisance to the dust of your feet."
Having thus recollected, one should cause [the disciple] to consume [the substance] while reciting "Ṛta, Gūṃ, Satya. As stated in the Bodhāyana-sūtra:

having washed the feet of the Blessed One, having filled a conch-shell vessel and other such vessels, having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, having offered the *caru* oblation, and having consecrated it with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge... [one should proceed].
Having performed the cleansing of the head with the two mantras, "kadrudrāya" and "mā tvā rudra," one should cause [the disciple] to consume [the substance] with the mantra "ṛtaṃ satyam.
Then, having worshipped [him] thoroughly and offered incense, [one addresses him as]: "O you whose form is consciousness, support of the universe!"

"O Sadāśiva, O Lord who abides in the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, accept this *nīrājana* known as the *avasara* (or *parā*). Having thus offered the secondary *nīrājana*, and having taken the fruit and other items, as well as the water from the *ānanda-pātra*, with the *ādhāra-pātra* and presented them; then [offer] the flower.
Having cast [the offering]:
"O Sadāśiva, sovereign of the waters of perfect consciousness-bliss, accept this lustration (nīrājana), O Lord Sadāśiva, which is called 'bathing'. Thus is the bathing lustration.

Having offered [the water] with splendor and sprinkled [him] with *vibhūti*, one should offer the *pādya* and other items as previously described. Then, having consecrated him with the *namaka* and other *rudra-sūktas*, and having given *ācamana* water, one should wipe him with a cloth, apply *vibhūti*, and accept the foot-water (*pādodaka*) as before. This is the foot-water which is an ancillary part of the bathing rite (*snapanakarmāṅga*).

Immediately after accepting [the offering], one should place a clear coal in a smokeless vessel made of iron or similar metal. Having applied a slight heating by means of the royal ritual protocol (*rājopacāra*), one should then place the aforementioned incense substances into the midst of the coals. Then, having performed the fanning with a fan and so forth, [one offers] the incense.

O Wealthy One, having offered to the beloved Liṅga this wondrous play known as "Awakening"— which spreads forth smoke, is renowned for the diffusion of incense, is endowed with the performance of the Wind-god through the clear observation of the large-limbed vessel, and is filled with immense bliss— place the sacrificial substance [therein].
Renowned by the name Cannamalleśa. || 1 ||

Having placed within the fire of one’s own heart—stirred by the vital breath (marut) inside the vessel of the body—that subtle reality endowed with the sixteen digits (kalās), which is being heated; [I offer this] to the Great One, the beloved, the manifest Prāṇaliṅga, renowned as the cause of all. [I offer it] into the clearly blazing fire, joined with the individual soul (jīva), wherein the state of the body as a vessel for the efficient cause has ceased.
The state of deep sleep is a manifested object consisting of the attainment of bliss;

it is the beloved, incomparable sign of the intense emotion, and is celebrated. I am the Supreme Śiva, the vessel of being, conceived within the limit of the state of *samarasa* (flavor-of-union); I have gathered [this] in the fire of Kṛṣṇa at the end of the fourth stage.
That one real entity, the Guru, the sky of consciousness, is eternally celebrated as having the singular form of Śiva.
Seated upon the peak of Śrīśaila, with the body of a bee, and with the tips of his two hands clearly manifesting devotion to the non-duality of Śiva,
he has cast away this entire living world— abounding in name, form, and action—
and fanned it with the great palm-leaf fan of the fearless gesture, shimmering in the hand of wisdom.
"O Śrī Cannamalleśvara, O Supreme Śiva, may there be happiness for this Liṅga consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātra) to which incense has been offered.
Having thus offered incense and placed its spreading [fragrance] upon the Liṅga, [he performs] the worship. 5. Then:
"O Mahādeva, O Pratyagātman, endowed with truth, consciousness, and bliss; O Īśa, accept this Nīrājana."

"O Sadāśiva, you who are named Maṅgala. Having thus offered the auspicious *nīrājana* and presented the garment, [he] offers the services (*upacāra*), namely, fragrant unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). [This is] the worship.

Having offered the services [of worship] by applying anointment with sandalwood and other substances; then, having performed the *nīrājana* (waving of lights) with camphor using the mantra: "O Sadāśiva, you who are beyond the unmanifest, the state of being, and the objects of the senses, beloved of all living beings—accept this *nīrājana* with camphor"; and then, having offered white *akṣata* grains.

O Worshipful One! Having offered flowers, leaves, garlands, and the ritual services (upacāras), [one should say]: "O Supreme Brahman, Great Liṅga, known as Bhāvaprāṇeṣṭa, O Lord Sadāśiva, accept this Nīrājana called Śṛṅgāra. Thus, having offered the Śṛṅgāra Nīrājana.
Then, having visualized his limbs and bestowed upon them the previously mentioned ornaments such as the crown,
[one should offer] the ritual services (upacāras) with various kinds of leaves and flowers as previously described, using the root mantra and the one hundred and eight names of Vṛṣabha.

Having recited and worshipped the names of the hosts of devotees—beginning with Rudra, the Pramatha Gaṇas, the leaders of the new and old four monasteries (caturmaṭha), and the Gurus—connected through the lineage, preceded by their names in the dative case (caturthyanta): [The worshipper says: "Obeisance to Śrī Vṛṣabheṃdra."
Oṃ, homage to Śivaṃkara. Oṃ, homage to Śiva. Homage to the leader of Śiva’s hosts.
Homage to him who was born from the mind of Śiva, whose body is the glorious True Dharma. To Śivadharma; to the most pure one; to the beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha; to the hero, the son of Śilāda.

To Śrīnandin, to Nandikeśvara, to him of beautiful gait; to the pure one; to the one who removes the pride of Viṣṇu’s vehicle (Garuḍa); to the one whose feet are the Vedas; to the one with hair like serpents; to the manifest supreme power; to the one of great body; to the one whose hump is Mount Mahāmeru; to the one possessing a white form; to the one with a red seat; to the one with red horns.
To the one with red eyes; to the stainless one; to the one whose nature is Dharma; to the well-minded one;

to the bestower of auspiciousness; to the maker of auspiciousness; to the devotee; to the lover of devotees; to the giver of devotion; to the beloved of devotion; to the second Śaṅkara; to the one of divine majesty; to the one adorned with divine ornaments; to the one who moves as a living being.

To the giver of liberation; to the one who bestows peace and self-restraint (40); to the all-pervading Lord; to Him whose every limb is smeared with ashes; to the one with the eye on His forehead; to the destroyer of worldly existence; to the Sun-like One; to the Blessed One; to the Auspicious One; to the great physician for the disease of worldly existence; to the one who is free from the net of fruits arising from the seven crores of great mantras.
To the destroyer of disease; to the destroyer of sin; to the destroyer of rebirth; to the Lord of the worlds;

to the creator of the world; to the Lord of the Blessed One; to the savior from the ocean of dissolution; to the purifier; to the sovereign of the Pramathas; to the Supreme Self; to the treasure-house of compassion; to the one liberated from bonds; to eternal bliss.

To the eternal one; to him whose splendor is like that of the moon; to the preceptor of Sanatkumāra and others; to the great witness; to the source of great prosperity; to him who is free from the six waves of worldly existence; to the virtuous one; to the destroyer of the essence of saṃsāra; to the stainless one; to the eternally auspicious one; to the eternal one.
To the one who is eternally festive; to the Guru; to the one free from lethargy; to the partless; to the infinite; to the supportless;
to the one whose intellect is free from conceptual construction; 60. To the boat for the ocean of worldly existence; to the one known through Vedānta; to the ocean of compassion;
to the one worshipped by Brahmā and the other deities; to the one whose body is the five-syllabled mantra; to the Supreme.
To him who has created the near and far shores; to him who is beyond the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa); to the imperishable one; to the one of great sound; to the Great Lord (Maheśa);

to the one with a vast belly; to the captivating one; to the destroyer of the intoxicated Daityas; to the God; to the one free from the possession of envy; to the omniscient one; O Lord of all lords, Sovereign of Samādhi!

To the one endowed with the conceit of Śiva; to the one devoted to the dharma of Śiva; to the protector of devotees; to the one whose body is his devotee; to the illustrious Bhasaveśvara; to the one who is ever-present; to the treasure-house of consciousness; to the one whose form is the letters of the alphabet; to the accomplisher of all goals. || 108 ||
Thus, one should worship with these one hundred and eight names: Salutation to the hosts of Rudras.
Salutation to the hosts of Pramathas. Salutation to the hosts of great devotees, both ancient and modern.
Salutation to the hosts of devotees linked in succession by the lineage of Gurus from the four monasteries. [Salutation] to the one named Vṛṣabha...

The Root Text: The illustrious Lord of Bulls, the bringer of auspiciousness; Śiva, the leader of the hosts of Śiva; born from the mind of Śiva, whose form is the glorious True Dharma; the banner of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, the most beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha; the heroic son of Śilāda, the illustrious Nandin, the Lord of Nandikeśvara.
He whose gait is most beautiful, who is pure, who removes the pride of Viṣṇu’s vehicle (Garuḍa),
whose feet are the Vedas, whose tail is the serpent, and who is the manifest Supreme Lord.
Possessing a massive body like Mount Meru, with a form as white as a hump,
he has a red face, red horns, and red eyes, yet is free from all stain.

He whose nature is the Dharma, who is well-disposed, the bestower of auspiciousness, the maker of good; he who is devoted, dear to his devotees, the giver of devotion, and compassionate toward his devotees.
The second is Śaṅkara, possessed of divine majesty and divine ornaments;
he is the moving being, the giver of liberation, the all-pervading lord who bestows peace and self-restraint.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, possessing a third eye on his forehead, he is the remover of worldly existence;
he is the divine Sun, the auspicious one, the great physician for the disease of saṃsāra.
He who is free from the net of fruits arising from the seven crores of great mantras,
the destroyer of disease, the destroyer of sin, the destroyer of rebirth, and the Lord of the worlds.
The creator of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, the savior from the ocean of dissolution,
the purifier, the lord of the Pramathas, the Supreme Self, and the treasure-house of compassion.
He is eternally free from bonds, infinite, perpetual, possessing the splendor of the moon,
the preceptor of Sanatkumāra and others, the witness of all, and the great exaltation.
The Guru is free from the six waves, virtuous, the destroyer of the essence of saṃsāra,
stainless, eternally auspicious, eternal, and ever-celebrating.
Free from drowsiness, partless, infinite, without foundation, and possessing a non-conceptual intellect;
the Vedānta is the one who prevents falling into the ocean of worldly existence, the object to be known, and the ocean of compassion.
He is the one to be worshipped by the deities beginning with Brahmā, the supreme being whose body is the five syllables.
The creator whose face looks toward both this shore and the further shore, who is beyond the bonds of individual souls (paśu-pāśa), the imperishable one;
the one of great roar, the Great Lord, the one with a vast belly, the captivating one.
The Lord is the slayer of the intoxicated Daityas, free from the influence of envy;
he is omniscient, a knower of all scriptures, the sovereign of all, and possessed of meditative absorption.
Endowed with the sense of identity as Śiva, devoted solely to the dharma of Śiva,
the protector of devotees, whose very body is his devotee, is the illustrious Lord Basava.
The treasure of consciousness, whose form is the phonemes, is the accomplisher of all goals;
and the one hundred and eight names of Ṛṣabha have been proclaimed.

The previously mentioned [articles]: the parasol, the fly-whisk, the palm-leaf fan, the mirror, the sound of bells, and the conch shell—these are the sixteen offerings (*upacārāṇi*). Having placed each according to its respective ritual procedure, one should then perform a song accompanied by cymbals made of bell-metal or similar materials, preceded by auspicious verses on the union of the *liṅga* and its limbs (*liṅgāṅgasaṃyoga*).

Just as in the ritual of the lamp-offering, my friend has entered my mind through the power of her mantra— such a thing performed out of compassion by the Guru himself— wherein the vital breath (marut) is established in Mallikārjuna.

The Guru [says]: When the venerable Lord of Teachers placed that which brings auspiciousness within his lotus-hand—the birth of Him who is inaccessible to the Vedas, who is like an unblinking eye situated within the mass of consciousness, and who is devoid of sense-objects—[he] respectfully praised that glory which shines when whispered into the ear in secret. || 1 || Rahasi karṇeritaṃ rājitaṃ... [The rest of the verse follows].

That Name, submerged in the basket of the wind of the light heart, has danced in various forms within all the courtyards of the lotus-forest of the senses; O you who have attained the state of relishing the essence of objects through the tongue,
that Name has become the fragrance of consciousness on the path of the Gandhavaha (wind).
The Guru [performs] the expansion of the swift-moving breath through the nostrils and outwards. (3) Having played musical instruments by means of mouth-blown instruments and the like,

(17) and having performed a dance preceded by the utterance of the seven notes as prescribed in the *Bharata-śāstra*, (18) he [offers] flowers and other items with his right hand, preceded by meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*).

Having visualized the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) [as described in verse] 19, and having performed the ritual service (upacāra), one should perform salutation with the mantras beginning with "Namo 'stu nīlagrīvāya" and ending with "Haṃtebhyo karaṃ namaḥ. Then, from "Namostvācāraliṅgāya" up to "Namo mahātmyaliṅgina," one should offer salutations.
One should recite from "To Śiva" and "I take refuge in Śiva," etc., up to "The illustrious Someśa of Aipura," etc., ending with "Pervaded by light beyond qualities. || 20 ||
The word *namaḥ* is Umā herself, and the word *śiva* is Śiva himself;
the word *āya* is their union—we worship that essence of Soma.
"O Uma, Śiva’s very limb; he himself is united with her;
Soma is their relationship"—thus we worship these three words.
We address you with auspicious words, O Lord of the Mountain,
so that this entire living world may be free from disease and well-disposed toward us.
Salutations to you, Śambhu, whose form is the Brahman in six abodes, of auspicious fame, perceivable by one's own self, beloved in the heart, and whose nature is pure knowledge.

Salutations to the Brahman of the six planes, whose singular nature is the single reality of the union between the Liṅga and the Aṅga, and who is the Reality attained through the yoga of devotion and knowledge.
Your self is the mind of the Mountain-born Goddess; Your attendants are the vital breaths; Your body is the house;
Your worship is the arrangement for the enjoyment of sense objects; Your state of sleep is meditative absorption (samādhi);
the movement of Your feet is the rite of circumambulation; and all Your speech is hymns of praise.
O Śambhu, whatever action I perform, all of it is for Your worship.

The true devotee [is established] in the *liṅga* that is the support of liberation, the *liṅga* of dense and stainless consciousness-form, the *liṅga* that is fully complete, the *liṅga* of the vital breath, the *liṅga* of the ever-constant and dense mind, the *liṅga* of the radiating state of being,
the *liṅga* whose self is the five Brahmans, and the *liṅga* of the syllable Om, which is light that effects the supreme station.
May my heart dwell eternally upon the Siddha-liṅga, the emblem of absolute liberation.

O Śiva, O Mahādeva, Lord of Bhavānī! Through worship of You there is *sārūpya* (attainment of Your form); through the chanting of "Śiva, Mahādeva" there is *sāmīpya* (proximity); through association with and conversation with those who are foremost among the devotees of Śiva there is [the same];
and through meditation on Your body composed of the moving and the unmoving, there is *sālokya* (residing in the same world).
O Lord, that which was appropriate for me has been accomplished here; I have achieved my purpose.
O Lord, you are not satisfied by three prostrations, nor by rituals of worship, nor by meditations and concentrations;
rather, you speak of pleasure through bows, clubs, and the eight [magical powers]. Therefore, I shall act accordingly.
Skilled in action, Dakṣa, Lord of Sacrifice, and protector of embodied beings, you performed the office of priest for the Ṛṣis; O Giver of Refuge, the hosts of Asuras were subdued by you.
For those devoted to the performance of sacrifices and their fruits, the sacrifice itself is a remedy through you.
For sacrifices performed by one devoid of faith certainly lead only to malevolent magic.
O Lord, having abandoned the path of the virtuous which is accessible through the Vedas, having uprooted both compassion for the earth and the affection intensified by ties to one's own kin,
this twice-born man has committed a grievous offense against you in debate.

Having praised him with such verses as, "He did not abandon his human state even while immediately undergoing transformation into a god," [the worshipper offers incense]. Immediately thereafter, [one offers incense] as before, reciting: "O Lord of Cannamalle, you whose heart is enveloped in the fragrance of the incense of the mind and other faculties ignited by the fire of consciousness; salutations to you! Thus, one offers incense as previously described.

Having offered [the lamp] with a ghee-lamp, one should perform the Great Lustration (*mahānīrājana*) with the mantra: "O Śambhu, O Śaṅkara, you who are full of consciousness and bliss, eternal, beyond qualities, and immovable—I shall offer this Great Lustration unto you. Having thus performed the Great Lustration, one should offer small lamps made of rice-flour and other materials, accompanied by the resounding sound of flickering lights.
May there be auspiciousness for the Liṅga of Mallikārjuna, known as Maṅgalacaṇḍa, which extends as far as the Vīradugdha fruit.

May there be auspiciousness for the enemy of Śamana (Yama), whose body is embraced by the creeper of consciousness appearing as a radiant flash of lightning, and who possesses the *liṅga* of Cannamalleśa.
Salutations to Hara, the charioteer of Madana, who is of the nature of Sat-Cit-Ānanda, whose form consists of the six *liṅgas* and limbs, and who is the *liṅga* of Cannamalleśa.
May there be auspiciousness for you, the powerful Guru, the master of the Pramathas, who exists in the form of a *liṅga*, a yogi of Śiva, the source of all, whose very self is auspiciousness.
To the reflection of the venerable Guru, who is of the nature of consciousness and whose self is Śiva.
May there be auspiciousness for Śrī Guheśa, who is the very life-breath of Śrī Giri.
"Not this, not this"—the meaning of "not" is that its form is like a body or a sense organ, which are as unstable as a bow.

Obeisance to You, the dense Liṅga who is the sun of consciousness placed in the lotus of Your hand, who shines forth as the blissful expanse of consciousness, and who is the source of supreme auspiciousness. O Three-eyed One!
O you whose body is pure consciousness alone, we offer auspicious praise to you, our Guru.
O Buddha, who churns the nectar of the moon, who has burnt away all sins with the fire of wisdom,
whose body is the Hari-liṅga, may there be auspiciousness for you from that Guru.
May there be auspiciousness for you from that Guru, Candraśekharasvāmīnātha, who reveals the yoga of the Tripuṭī situated above the deep cavity of the moon.
Having offered these verses as lamps for the hands, [he says]: May there be auspiciousness for my chosen Liṅga;

may there be auspiciousness for the Liṅga of Cannamalleśa—may there be auspiciousness for my chosen Liṅga! May there be auspiciousness for my chosen Liṅga, whose form is fashioned from the tender sprouts of the tree’s hands; may there be auspiciousness for my chosen Liṅga, the swift arrow of the moment of devotion!
To Him who has cast down His body, whose form is the manifestation of the syllables, who is all-pervading, whose body is bound by the mind and vital breaths of His devotees,
who is beautifully adorned by the enjoyment of the limbs of His devotees; to my beloved one,

whose fair-limbed form is intent upon the network of the eyes of His devotees, who is destined to grant the desires of His devotees, and who, like a parrot in a beautiful cage, dwells within the hearts of His devotees.
May You, who are the object of the supreme devotion of the faithful, grant me Your grace.
O You whose heart is ever-enveloped by the spreading radiance of the gaze of Your devotees, who shine with a mind intent upon them;

O You who are like a young cuckoo to those whose souls are devoted, and who are the tender sprout for the vine of the true object of devotion—may You grant me Your grace. (3) May You grant me Your grace.

Having offered various kinds of auspicious songs such as these, and having presented *āratrikas* made from rice-flour (*śālipiṣṭa*) in the shape of hand-drums (*ḍamaru*), and having moved [the deity] while waving lamps at its sides, behind, and in front— [thus] performing the worship— grant supreme devotion unto Your feet.
O Someśvara, embodiment of compassion, grant me unwavering [devotion]; beyond this, I desire nothing else.
O abode of compassion, O garden of compassion, O mine of compassion, O ocean of compassion! O bond of compassion, O ornament of compassion, protect me!

May this embodied form of Śambhu, whose linga is directly present and perceived like a dolphin-tailed flame, which very slowly and from all sides manifests its own intensely dense power of splendor in the form of a pillar of light— may He thus comprehend [the universe].
If, at the conclusion of my prārabdha karma, he acts out of compassion for me as he has done for you; so it is with me.

"O Śambhu, by Your grace, please grant me this boon: that at the time of my end, I may generally be dissolved into this Liṅga of Yours, which is His supreme radiance, along with my very body. Having made this petition with such verses, [he should pray]. 22.
These functions of the senses have arisen within me, each in its own respective domain;
yet, O Essence of Non-duality, I am not one who would dare to cause even a moment’s interruption to the arrival of peace.
O Mandarā, if that which was disregarded is unknown, and everything else is unknown, then all that is other than you is likewise unknown; therefore, O Lord of Umā, [reveal] that to me.
While this body of mine stands in the palm of my hand within the self-luminous liṅga of the Supreme Self, it remains hidden;
the cause for this wonder is like a piece of gold remaining unseen within the womb of a fire-pit.

Having made this request: "May this Linga of mine—pure and fragrant with camphor, the limb of Śiva, established here in the form of a lamp of innate radiance—become fearless through the yoga of my own devotion and, at the end, be dissolved into the state of the Great Guru. If one is incapable of performing the appropriate services, [one should simply say]: "Obeisance! (namaḥ).

"Śivāya"—this single verse is the coral [bead]. Thereafter, the worship known as *naivedya* (the food offering) should be performed; its procedure is now stated. Now, among all the ritual services (*upacāra*) of worship, the primary form, the offering of *naivedya*, is described. In the initial rite of offering the chosen *liṅga*, [one should offer] into the vessel of Śiva with the root mantra.

Having set aside the *vibhūti*, and in accordance with the scriptural injunction that "food equal in measure to the guru's meal, together with vegetables, [should be placed] in the vessel," one should, after depositing the side dishes (*vyañjana*), foods to be chewed (*bhakṣya*), foods to be eaten (*bhojya*), foods to be licked (*lehya*), foods to be sucked (*coṣya*), drinks, and so forth,
each into their respective vessels as appropriate, proceed with the *śaraṇa* [mantra].
From the mouth of the cook [emerge] the aforementioned four kinds of food substances,

including soups and side dishes prepared with the six flavors, as well as mixed flavors combined with substances such as milk, curd, buttermilk, ghee, the juice of *tintriṇī*, and molasses-water, each in its respective mixed form.

Having heard the yoga, one employs the hand of one’s own sense of hearing to offer that sense organ to one’s chosen deity (iṣṭaliṅga), using the names of its constituent parts— namely, those mixed with side-dishes possessing pungent, bitter, sour, sweet, salty, and astringent flavors— and thus experiences the bliss of its grace.

Having offered one's own physical eyes as an instrument for the eyes of one's chosen *liṅga*— which are the forms of that [divine] object— thereby experiencing the bliss of beholding His grace; and at the time of meditating upon that object, having offered one's own mental faculty as an instrument for the mental offering to one's chosen *liṅga*.
Experiencing the bliss of beholding His grace, at the time of contact and union with the reality of His feet,
one offers one’s own hands— whether soft, hard, cold, or warm— to the hand-faculty of one’s chosen *liṅga*.

Having performed [this], while experiencing the pleasure of touching each respective object, one should perform the threefold offering—by means of body, mind, and speech—at the time of offering each respective prasāda, according to the statement: "The offering is auspicious through the threefold [means]. Thus, it is the threefold offering.

This must be performed. He describes the threefold division of *arpaṇa*: if the five types of food—grains, roots, fruits, leaves, and vegetables—as well as condiments and liquid substances such as milk, curd, and ghee, are repeatedly touched with one's own hand and offered to one's chosen *liṅga*, that action is considered "performed through ritual action" (*kriyākṛtam*).

It becomes mixed with various kinds of substances— eatables, chewables, lickables, suckables, and drinks— and from the distress of others, it takes on the form of various soups and various cooked foods; it becomes the finest grains within the water of that broth, and it reaches the state of being the seeds within those fruits, all gathered together by those various condiments.

The creeper is illuminated by the distinctions of acceptance and rejection; it is mixed with the faint radiance of fire, sun, and moon; it is mixed with shadows; it is mixed with atoms of wind, fire, and earth; it is mixed with space; it is mixed with atoms of air; it is mixed with external air, internal air, and intermediate air; and it is mixed with the fragrance of flowers, fruits, and incense.
The varieties— incense, smoke, fire, steam mixed with water, mixed with cooked food, mixed with flavor,

mixed with color, mixed with form, and mixed with relish— become mental action performed by offering them in turn to one's own chosen *liṅga*, preceded by the contemplation of the enjoyment of that *liṅga*.

Whatever foods there may be—such as rice cooked with milk, cakes, mung beans, and various soups; whatever condiments are mixed therein, such as salt, sugar, sweet juices, black pepper, alkaline substances, tamarind fruit, sour preparations, cardamom, camphor, and various fragrant ingredients; as well as milk and curd.

The essences such as clarified butter, the various substances appropriate for each specific occasion as far as they are available, and their respective mixtures and so forth, are explained by first uttering their names; likewise, at the time of offering one’s own desired action, speech, and deed to the Lord, it is done with devotion.

Because it is a conventional usage such as "one desires the *liṅga*," one should recall the path of dependence upon oneself regarding the meanings of those words; then, following the sequence of their arrangement,
just as there is satisfaction with the various categories of word-meanings, one should likewise utter the names of the respective mixed substances and so forth.

One should offer each type of substance in sequence eight times: once with the root mantra, six times with the names of the six limbs beginning with Ācāra, and once again by reciting the names of the six limbs. In between these offerings, one should present water, incense, and so forth.

One should offer [the offering] with the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that it is "the cow" (*goga*). Regarding this, the power of offering the primary form of the *naivedya* has been taught by Śiva in the *Paramarahasya* and other tantras,
and by the venerable Māyidevācārya in works such as the *Anubhavasūtra* and the *Viśeṣārthaprakāśa*.
That which was correctly composed by the venerable Cannabasaveśvara and others in works such as the *Miśārpaṇa* through the prescription of surrendering body,
instruments, and being; and that which was widely proclaimed in many ways by the venerable Somanārādhya in the *Prasāda-prakaraṇa* section of the *Basavarājīya-bhāṣya*, is likewise written here.

They say that the *nirmālya* (remnants) of the Śiva-liṅga is of six kinds: the property of the deity, the substance belonging to the deity, the food offering (*naivedya*), that which has been offered, the substance for Caṇḍeśvara, and likewise that which has been cast outside; such is the sixfold *nirmālya*.
The property of the gods is known from the Smṛti as consisting of village lands and the like, four types of male and female slaves,
gold, silver, gems, and so forth.
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, water, food, drink, or other such items one intends for the deity— all that is proclaimed as *naivedya* (an offering).

This threefold [offering] is worthy of honor: likewise, the garlands, perfumes, food, drink, and so forth that have been enjoyed by Śiva are declared to be "nivedita" (offered), which supremely removes all sins.
In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a mobile liṅga, a metal liṅga, a jewel liṅga, a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga,
and in all images, there shall be no appointment of a Caṇḍa.
When the *liṅga* has been installed according to the prescribed rite by all the gods, asuras, and men,
O Śivā, these three kinds of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) are placed under the authority of Caṇḍeśa.
For that which is cast outside is indeed unfit [for use] due to its being a different substance;
moreover, all piśācas always have the right [to it].
Thus, among the six kinds of *prasāda*, only that which has been offered (*nivedita*) is fit for those who consume the *prasāda*.

They say that this offered *prasāda* is of two kinds: that which is to be eaten (*bhojya*) and that which is to be worn (*dhārya*). "To be eaten" is an illustration for things such as food to be chewed, licked, drunk, and so forth. As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The remains of offerings (nirmālya) are said to be of two kinds: food and drink, and ornaments.
In the Śrīliṅga Purāṇa: One should accept fruits, flowers, fragrances, garments, and ornaments offered to the Liṅga; otherwise, it shall result in sin.
Whatever food—whether to be chewed, licked, or sucked—is auspiciously offered to the Liṅga, it becomes a grace (prasāda);
however, if it is mixed with leftover food, that grace shall be fruitless.
Even if one eats a great deal or even a small amount mixed with the food of the learned,
yet not offered [to the deities], one likewise incurs the sin of arrogance.

Regarding this matter, there is also a scriptural authority (*śruti*): "They eat the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*); one should eat only the remains of the offering," and so forth. Based on such scriptural and traditional authorities (*āgama*), the entire collection of items—including food remnants from vessels and the like—must be avoided.
Whatever foods there may be—solid foods, coverings, drinks, and grains—all those should be offered to Śambhu; one should not eat them oneself, but rather out of a sense of servitude.

In the venerable *Liṅga-purāṇa*, it is said: "Whatever foods—whether to be chewed, licked, or sucked—are offered to the Liṅga, one should eat them as the remnants of the Liṅga; these are declared to be its grace (*prasāda*)."
Sugarcane, pieces of fruit, cakes, edibles, and condiments—only that which is a gracious gift (prasāda) should be eaten; anything else is equal to cow-flesh or excrement.
One should offer sugarcane, plantains, fruits, and the like with pieces of sugar;
one should offer grapes, dates, and mangoes without pieces of sugar.

Having offered these and other items— such as food to be chewed, swallowed, licked, drunk, and sucked— to the Śiva-liṅga only once, one should partake of that alone as *prasāda*. Having placed a limited amount of food, according to one's own requirement, into the vessel of the liṅga, one should offer it to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭaliṅga*).
Some say that it is not fit to be done; however, that is not so.

Having placed one's own food—limited in quantity and consumed from the vessel of the *liṅga*—into the *liṅga* only once, if that [food] is offered to the *liṅga* with each individual morsel, it does not constitute a contradiction.

He states the distinctions regarding the offering of those items: foods to be chewed (*bhakṣya*), foods to be swallowed (*bhojya*), foods to be licked (*lehya*), foods to be sucked (*coṣya*), and drinks (*pānīya*);
juices such as milk, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and oil; side dishes (*vyañjana*) such as tubers, roots, fruits, leaves, vegetables, and soups;
various kinds of cooked rice such as milk-rice, mung-bean rice, and śāli-rice; and grapes.

Having placed plantains, mangoes, and other fruits— various types of substances endowed with the six tastes, as available and appropriate for each particular time— into the vessel of her chosen *liṅga*,
she then heard the names of those substances from the mouth of the cook at that moment: pungent, bitter, sour, sweet, and alkaline.

Having offered the names of flavors— mixed with various condiments and accompanied by astringent tastes— to his own sense of hearing by means of the hand of that very sense, he becomes worthy of hearing the bliss resulting from its grace.

By means of the hand of one's own visual faculty, one offers the form of that object (the *tatpadārtha*) to the visual faculty of one's chosen deity (*sveṣṭaliṅga*); through its grace, one becomes worthy of experiencing the bliss of beholding it. At the time of the manifestation of that object, by means of the hand of one's own mind, [one offers it] to the mind of one's chosen deity.
Having performed the act of offering (*samarpaṇa*), one becomes worthy of experiencing the bliss of contemplating that grace (*prasāda*).
At the time of touching and uniting with the substance of that [grace], by offering one’s own soft, hard, cold,
or warm palms into the palms of one’s chosen *liṅga*, one receives that respective grace.

He becomes worthy of experiencing the bliss of direct contact. At the time of offering that grace, whatever merit has been offered through the threefold means of action, mind, and speech—if one enjoys [the fruit] without having offered it, the grace would be rendered fruitless. On the basis of such scriptural authority as this, there must be that threefold offering.

This must indeed be performed at all times. Regarding that, he explains the threefold division of offerings: the five kinds of edible grains and other foods, bulbs, roots, fruits, various vegetables and condiments, and liquid substances such as milk, curd, and ghee—all these various categories of items upon one's own palm, after repeatedly touching each one.

If that action is offered to one’s own chosen *liṅga*, then that rite becomes truly performed. It includes various kinds of foods— edibles, chewables, lickables, drinks, and suckables— mixed together with diverse soups and various cooked dishes, along with the successive grains of rice contained therein.

The various distinctions of accepting and rejecting— such as clusters of *mudga* beans mixed with various seasonings, seeds contained within fruits, and creepers and the like— are illuminated. [These include] Nala,
the sun, moonlight, mixed shadows, and those belonging to the aerial, fiery, and earthly elements.
The distinctions consist of atoms mixed with space, atoms mixed with wind, wind mixed with external wind,

and the fragrance of flowers, fruits, and incense mixed with passion, mixed with form, and mixed with taste; these are offered to one's chosen deity (*sveṣṭaliṅga*) in succession, preceded by the contemplation of the enjoyment of the *liṅga*.

It is produced by mental activity (*mānasakriyā*). Whatever there may be— whether boiled rice and so forth, baked cakes and the like, or various forms such as mung beans and other legumes— within those various side dishes (*vyañjana*) are placed sea salt,
sugar and the like for sweetness, black pepper and the like for pungency, alkaline substances, the juice of *tintriṇī* fruit and the like for acidity, and cardamom, camphor and the like.
Having offered substances such as milk, curd, ghee, and other juices, as well as whatever varieties of articles are available and appropriate for that time,
if these are offered after first uttering their respective names and dedicating them to one's chosen deity (iṣṭaliṅga),
the act becomes a formal ritual offering (kriyākṛta). Following those three types of offerings, at the time of accepting each respective prasāda:

"One should offer the form (rūpa) and also offer the relish (ruci); for if both offerings are lacking, grace (prasāda) becomes fruitless"— according to this authoritative statement, one should place the relish contained within each respective substance into the vessel of one's own tongue-faculty and, by means of the mental faculty, [offer it] to one's chosen *liṅga*.

Having offered the sense organ of the tongue, one becomes worthy of experiencing the delight therein. Otherwise, it describes the act of taking [the offering] away; in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pitāmaha, it says: "The food offering (*naivedya*), though placed at a distance, has been accepted by me through the mere sight of it."
"O Kalodbhava, I consume the flavors from the tip of the devotee's tongue"—

from such authoritative statements as these, [it is understood that] by whatever action or word [is performed] upon the tip of the tongue of Śiva-bhakta-s who are solely devoted to Śiva and intent on the practice of the Vīra-vrata, [the fruit belongs to the Prāṇaliṅga].

That very offering becomes dedicated to Śiva when it is offered with a mind focused on the internal delight found within the form of the substance previously presented according to the prescribed words, and with a deliberate intent that disregards one's own tongue. Indeed, at that very moment,
even if there is a prohibition regarding smelling or touching during the state of cooking, [the offering remains pure].

Even if it has been handled by attendants, it remains an offering to Śiva; for as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Whatever object has been smelled, touched, or seen with a pure mind and offered to Śiva, not even the slightest thing in it is defiled."
The surrendering of one's own independence regarding various objects does not lead to contradiction.
Even that man who does not cultivate purity toward the *Kriyātilaka*, the *Śuddhaśaiva*,
and the *Prasāda* goes to a terrible, inexhaustible hell for an eon.
Just as there is no prior mental cultivation for a well-established *liṅga*,
so too one should not recall a previous name for the grace of Śiva.
The ghee residing within the bodies of cows may not serve as their own ornament,
yet when transformed into a form suited for ritual use, it becomes their medicine;
likewise, the Supreme Lord, though dwelling within the body, is like one who drinks [the essence].
And without worship, the Lord does not bestow welfare upon the king.
Based on the authority of such statements, some maintain that external offerings alone are sufficient.
"The mind itself is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
for just as a son embraces [his mother], a husband is not so embraced."
Based on this statement, some say that internal offering alone is sufficient;

however, that is not so. For according to the authority of the scriptural and traditional statements in the Yajurveda—namely, "What one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks through speech, and that one performs through action"—there must be the communication of the word.

The mental cultivation is the act of dedication; that which is purified through the three instruments (of body, speech, and mind)—whether it be external or internal—is indeed the dedication to the God. In the *Kātyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*, while walking on a path, one recites the mantra:
"Homage to Rudra who dwells in the waters! Grant me well-being; [grant me] the forest."

While walking, he recites the mantra: "Homage to Rudra, O Lord of the Forest; grant us well-being and bring it to fulfillment. When moving through water, he recites the mantra: "Homage to Rudra, the dweller in the waters; grant us well-being and bring it to fulfillment. Therefore, whatever action one may be performing, one should always do so with the thought: "Homage to Rudra."

The meaning of this is as follows: one who travels along a path equipped with sandals, or for the sake of their pleasure mounted on a horse, a swing, an elephant, or another vehicle, should— preceded by the consecration with the mantra "Namo Rudrāya"— offer the act of going and coming upon that path to the deity residing on the path (*pathiṣad*).

"Obeisance to the Lord of travelers! O Lord of the paths, who protects the wayfarers on their journeys, please protect my own people and fulfill the ease of their coming and going. Having made this petition, he proceeds by placing his trust at every step upon the paths of grace through that Lord's favor. In that manner...

Returning again, as he goes toward the forest and enters it at the time of departure, he experiences the pleasures of the shade and sunlight, the cold and heat within that forest, and the joys of beholding the shadows of various trees— those which have sprouted, put forth shoots, budded, flowered, and borne fruit— as well as their respective blossoms, leaves, and fruits.
Having offered the pleasures of experiencing fragrances, and the joys of hearing various soft, sweet, and tender sounds from parrots, cuckoos, bees, swans, peacocks, and other birds,
to the Lord of the Forest, the Lord of Trees, the Lord of Narratives.
Having made this request—“Svasti! Grant me success through the name of the Lord of Names;
fill me with the bliss of His grace”—one becomes worthy of partaking in that grace and of experiencing the bliss of grace consisting in entering and departing from those various forests of grace.

At the time of immersion, having first consecrated the water with the mantra "Namo Rudrāya," and having performed the entry into and exit from that respective water while offering the pleasure of its coolness and warmth, [one recites]: "Obeisance to the one who dwells in the waters; obeisance to Śiva."

"Salutations to him who goes to heaven and to him who does not; salutations to him who carries across and to him who leads beyond. Having thus petitioned, "O Lord of Waters, grant me well-being and establish me in the bliss of that grace," one becomes worthy to experience the bliss of receiving that gracious water.
Therefore, while performing any action whatsoever, one should do so thinking, "This is all an offering to Rudra.

In every case, both externally and internally, having offered the form of the substance to the external [liṅgas] and its formlessness to the internal ones, one should also offer the very relish (*ruci*) of the substance. Thus, that which is devoid of this twofold offering—
If that clarity of mind were fruitless, [it would contradict the following]: In the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
"Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse—he who has his mind offered to Śiva and possesses devotion is [liberated], and not otherwise."
Whether in unions or in separations, he who would perform even the slightest acts of pleasure while remaining constantly attentive before the image of his chosen deity;
In the Vātūlatantra, whatever ritual action was previously set forth as to be performed,
that very one the wise one should perform, O Mahādeva, with a mind intent on dedication.
Whatever object is presented before one for enjoyment,
that very thing should be offered to the deity and accepted by those intent on devotion.
Whatever happiness arises from the senses, that is offered to Śiva; it should be experienced through the grace of Him and by means of those very senses.

Likewise, having properly offered the pleasures derived from the objects of touch, form, sound, taste, and smell— which have come through the senses of skin, eye, ear, tongue, and nose— to one's chosen deity with a focused mind and through the firm resolve of the self; immediately thereafter—
One becomes worthy to experience the bliss of its grace.
That which arises from the gateway of the senses should proceed from the gateway of the senses;
if it is enjoyed by another sense, it is as unworthy as an ornament [placed on the wrong limb].
"By Rudra they eat what is eaten; by Rudra they drink what is drunk; by Rudra they smell what is smelled"—such is the definition, and so forth. This is the method:
he who, having commenced [the ritual], should employ all actions endowed with qualities and all entities.
In their absence, there is the destruction of performed karma; upon the exhaustion of karma, another [agent] goes forth as the one who delivers it.
Thus ends the statement of Vātūla as spoken by Śiva. This is an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the *Mantrōpaniṣad*. In the *Kriyātilaka*:
"Having reached that which was unattainable and having attained it, one should indeed perform the placement (*sthāna*) in the improper place;
one who thoroughly understands these two [states] is gracious and vigilant."

A man devoted to the worship of Śiva should never, under any circumstances, enjoy any object whatsoever without first offering it to the Lord. Ritual service should extend at least to the lighting of lamps, while worship should extend at least to the presentation of food offerings (naivedya).
Therefore, if the food offering (naivedya) is lacking, the worship will always be deficient.
The offering of food (naivedya) is said to conclude with the enjoyment of that very grace;
if it is offered without the distribution of grace, even though it has been presented, it is fruitless.
If there is a lapse in worship or the favor [of the deity] due to any cause whatsoever— whether through vows, fasts, or observances— one does not obtain the fruit thereof,
even from thousands of fasts or hundreds of *prājāpatya* penances.
They are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of a grain of the grace of Śiva.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Liberation according to Śaṅkara comes through even a tiny fragment of the grace of that Rudra alone who is praised in all the Vedas."
One may not attain liberation merely by partaking of the grace of water from the feet, even if it were as much as a sixteenth part of a sesame seed or a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass.
One should not practice fasting or similar penances toward one who has received grace from a Prāṇaliṅgin;
if one should do so out of delusion, a great transgression will befall him.
There are many worshippers and devotees by the hundreds of thousands;
yet, among them, the recipients of grace are only two or three, and certainly not five or six.
Those people who, though endowed with devotion, revile those who enjoy the offerings of prasāda, go to hell together with their ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
The Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas, as well as the gods headed by Viṣṇu, know the greatness of Śiva’s grace; what then of mortal men?
Thus, it has been extensively set forth by the noble Somanātha in the *Miśrārpaṇā*, where the various divisions of the offering of body, instruments, and state (*bhāva*) have been delineated.
For fear of prolixity, it is not written here; it should be consulted in that very work. Likewise, in the *Anubhavasūtra*:
O Māyī, according to the *Sadbhāvādhikaraṇa* of Devācārya, one should enjoy only that form which has been offered into the *liṅga*;
another form must not be enjoyed, for if it were enjoyed, it would be as if it had never been offered.
Just as the act of eating proceeds sequentially in a person.
In this way, the sign of the act of offering proceeds sequentially;

from the beginning of the worship until its end, this [offering] occurs through devotion. Indeed, this body of the ritual object (padārtha-tanu) exists from the start of the worship until its conclusion, and thereafter, this very body of the ritual object becomes the body of grace (prasāda-tanu).

One should be devoted in worship; by the power of devotion, grace should be sought. After the conclusion of one worship, when the opportunity for the next act of worship arises on the path, whatever substance is offered there shall be auspicious.
However, that which is offered at the moment of one's own [personal] need is inauspicious, as it is not properly surrendered.
In another place, an offering given to a *liṅga* at the proper time (*velā*) shall be auspicious;
that which is given out of season (*anāvasarika*) is inauspicious, as it is not properly offered.
According to this statement, the offering of substances must be performed at the time of worshipping one's chosen *liṅga*.
Since that grace (*prasāda*) remains until the completion of the worship, it constitutes the body of the grace;

therefore, from the conclusion of the worship until the end of the mental worship (*mānasa-pūjā*), there is no offering of what has been given according to one's own desire—this is the meaning of the previous statement.

Because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no room for offering [the vibhūti] between the two acts of worship. Nevertheless, because the *prāṇaliṅga* is present within the body, and because the body itself is the *liṅga*, one should consider that the desire of the devotee is the very desire of the *liṅga*.
Having thus reflected, certain wise practitioners perform the worship with sacred ash and the water-vessel.
Having set aside the cooked substance, it is taken up; that we do not know, but the Lord knows.

Furthermore, regarding the consumption of the cooked substance, in worship, and in the eightfold ritual (aṣṭavidhārcana), having prepared some colored designs (raṅgavallī), that is offered. That too, O Śiva, the God, [is performed] thus by mind, speech, and body.
