Immediately after the threefold offering, at the time of accepting His grace, one should offer a form and then also offer a substance according to one's preference.
If both offerings are lacking, that grace will be fruitless.
The pure *prāṇaliṅga* is offered through the mouth, while the *iṣṭaliṅga* is offered externally.
Then they know that which is accomplished as truly established when it is offered through the signs of the [three] states (bhāvaliṅga).
Having received each respective grace through those various offerings,
the Self itself— the Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña— enjoys it with devotion.
In all states— waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth— and at all times,
this [soul] is undoubtedly untainted by the enjoyment offered to the *liṅga*.
Whatever is to be enjoyed in the three abodes, and whatever enjoyment there may be for the devotee— he who knows that threefold reality while eating is not defiled.

Just as one should respectfully perform for one's own enjoyment that which is to be done by means of substances appropriate to the time, obtained through chance, oneself, and with regard to the three genders.
Those who are experts in the single practice of renunciation say that the dedication of those actions is [the true offering];
for indeed, the objects of enjoyment for the self are of three kinds.
It is threefold, namely: that called the gross (sthūla), that called the dissolved (pravilīna), and that called bliss (ānanda).
The gross is the substance (dravya), while the dissolved is the form (rūpa) and the delight (ruc).
Ānanda, however, is satisfaction; these [other states] are distinct in their sequence:
the form [of bliss] occurs in the offering of external objects, while the relish occurs in the offering of internal objects.
In this context, satisfaction is said to consist precisely in the offering of one's own limbs;
for the universe, by its very nature, offers its forms and substances to the chosen liṅga.
In the case of the *prāṇaliṅga*, however, the offering consists of radiant substances directly;
in the *bhāvaliṅga*, O wise ones, it always consists of the offering of substances that grant satisfaction.
Thus it was said by Śilā in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"O Lotus-born One, the food offering placed before me has been accepted by me through the mere sight of it; I consume the flavors from the tip of the devotee's tongue."

Since it is well-established in all the scriptures through such statements that Śiva is satisfied by the vessel of the devotee’s tongue, at the time of accepting His grace, one should place the flavor inherent in each respective substance into the vessel of one’s own faculty of taste and, by means of the mental organ, [offer it] to one’s chosen *liṅga*.
Having offered the sense of the tongue [to the deity], one should eat everything without exception with full attention, until satisfaction arises through the relish of that grace. Thereafter,
remembering the application of unguents at the place called Reṇukaikya, one should apply a non-liquid unguent such as water and so forth to the limbs.
Having prepared this at that time—
regarding the body as the vessel, the senses as the utensils, and this individual soul as the substance which is the food—
offer it with devotion to the Liṅga; then partake of that grace (prasāda) which remains as his leavings.
"That supreme state which remains when [the world] is negated by 'not this,
not this,' because it cannot be negated— be happy, realizing 'I am that.'"
"I am not the non-self; who was I before? I am that very one who stands upon the plane as the witness of the Self.
I am the servant of Śiva, the Lord of that; thus one should conduct oneself with the higher modes of service, thinking, 'I am His servant.'"
Thus, the experiences expressed in these verses and others should be recollected following reflection (*manana*). [Pūjalu]

Immediately thereafter, having performed the ritual washing of the hands with water from the general *arghya* vessel held in the hand, and having applied the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) to the *liṅga*, [one should pray]: "O Eternal Supreme Brahman, whose form is consciousness and supreme bliss, O Īśa, Sadāśiva, accept this *nīrājana* known as Bliss."

Thus, O Ānanda, having performed the *nīrājana* rite and offered betel-leaf according to the previously mentioned method, one should thoroughly experience its flavor with the tongue of one’s own *liṅga*. [Then] the worshipper [should pray]: "Salutations to You, O Blessed One, who created Brahmā in the beginning," with these verses from the Rudra-sūkta.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should then proceed according to the sequence of offerings ending with the lamp (*dīpa*). Having thus offered the *nīrājana*—which consists of unbroken supreme bliss and the nature of awakening—to the Great Guru, who is the embodiment of the Guru and possesses infinite forms, with the words: "O Great Guru, O Treasure of Compassion, accept this immeasurable *nīrājana*," one should perform the *nīrājana* for the Guru.
Again, having assumed his splendor and put on his upper garment, he was intent on worship. || 12 || Pūjalu.

One should place within the casket the beloved *liṅga* in the form of Mallikārjuna—the very nature of the conscious witness (*sākṣin*) situated upon the seat of the lotus-hand—upon one's own body. [The offerings: 14.
The seat, the sacred thread, the fly-whisk, the song,
the hymn of praise, and the fragrant scents— these six varieties originate from Sadyojāta.
Invocation, garlands, fans, musical instruments, effort, and likewise unbroken rice grains—
these six varieties are proclaimed as originating from the Vāmadeva mantra.
Water for the feet, unguents, the mirror, dance, making known [the deity],
and the offering of flowers— these six are the rites of Aghora, which do not arise [in other forms].
The water offering (arghya), the ornaments, the ringing of the bell, the circumambulation, the dismissal (visarjana),
and the lighted ghee— these six originate from the Tatpuruṣa [mukha].
The sipping of water (ācamana), the parasol and conch, prostration,
the food offering (naivedya), and betel— these six originate from Īśāna;
first comes the sprinkling with sacred ash (vibhūti), and after that, the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Then there is the heating with charcoal, followed by fanning with incense;
then the spreading of incense and the covering with a cloth.
Arising from the union with the five Brahmās, they are declared to be six.
Having meditated correctly in the manner described above, one should worship the offerings of honor with their respective mantras.

Now, as for another mode of worship: having fashioned a lotus-shaped mandala with some colored powders (*raṅgavallī*), having worshipped it in its subtle form, and having offered fruit and other items along with water at the appropriate time—this concludes [the ritual].
[Thus ends the procedure for the worship of Śiva in the *Śrīvīraśaivasiddhāntottarakaumudī*.]
